name: Purple Grey
lede: Purple Grey is [[grey|Grey]] with a visible wash of purple in it, a muted, dusty lilac-grey named by combining two basic color words.

sections.title: Two basic color words combined
sections.body:
The name pairs the parent word [[grey|Grey]] with "purple" as a modifier, describing a grey pulled toward violet rather than naming a dye, a mineral or a place; it was recorded in Randall Munroe's 2010 xkcd color-naming survey [1]. No earlier dictionary or plate in the books consulted here carries this exact compound, though both words it combines are far older [1].

In printed English, the phrase "purple grey" (across all its uses, color and otherwise) rose fastest in the 1840s and peaked in the 1870s, a pattern about the words' broader use rather than this swatch specifically [2]. Its closest look-alikes on file are [[grey-purple|Grey Purple]], the same two words in the other order and purpler, and [[purplish-grey|Purplish Grey]], almost the same color, with [[old-lavender|Old Lavender]] and [[mountbatten-pink|Mountbatten Pink]] a little further out [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, finds a match for this lilac-grey in 27 of them, about 0.11 percent, rarer than 63 percent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 3.7 times the expected rate for that century (7 of 1,674 paintings from then), and inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 38 percent of cases, ranked by lightness rather than raw area [4].

The earliest match in our archive is a 1375 painting by Agnolo Gaddi, six hundred and thirty-five years before the name itself appears in 2010; our archive's early centuries are thin, so that date is a floor, not a first, and the match is only a look-alike hue in an aged, varnished photograph, not proof a matching pigment existed then [4].
